title: Simplified, High-throughput Analysis of Single-cell Contractility using Micropatterned Elastomers
protocol: Add 20 mL of F12 Ham's based medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) into a 50 mL conical tube.
Obtain a 24 well plate designed for cell contractility assays.
Peel the plastic film from the top of the plate and set it down carefully.
Aspirate the PBS layer from the wells using a vacuum aspirator, removing one row at a time until no longer completely full.
Carefully remove remaining PBS from each well.
Fill each well with 500 µL of cell culture medium, ensuring coverage across the bottom of the well without touching it.
Set the prepared plate aside after filling all wells with medium.
Retrieve the culture flask containing passage 7 or lower primary human bladder smooth muscle (BSM) cells from a 37 °C incubator.
Check cell morphology under a microscope to ensure cells have grown to at least 90% confluency but less than 100%.
Trypsinize the cells for 2.5 min until they are detached before quenching them with serum-supplemented medium (10% FBS).
Use a hemocytometer to count the cells and dilute the cell suspension to approximately 50,000 cells/mL in serum-supplemented medium.
Rapidly strain the cell suspension through a 40 or 100 µm cell strainer into a 50 mL conical tube with a serological pipette.
Add 500 μl of the 50,000 cells/ml cell suspension into each of the 24 wells on the plate using a P1000 pipette by dispensing the solution dropwise across different positions in the wells.
Let the plate sit at room temperature for 1 h to allow the cells to settle directly onto the micropatterns without becoming influenced by microcurrents generated by evaporation.
Place the plate into a 37 °C incubator overnight.
Create a six-step, eight-fold dilution series by transferring 30 µL of the stock drug into consecutive 210 µL volumes of DMSO and thoroughly mixing between each transfer step.
Mix 30 µL of blebbistatin with 470 µL of cell culture medium to achieve a 16.7-fold dilution of DMSO.
Transfer 200 µL of the intermediate solution into wells containing 100 µL of medium in a 24 well plate, yielding an additional six-fold dilution of DMSO.
Incubate the treated plate at 37 °C for 30 min.
Add Hoechst 33342 live nuclear stain solution to each well at a final concentration of 1:10,000.
Allow the staining to incubate for an additional 15 min.
Access a microscope equipped with imaging channels for both cell nuclei (DAPI) and micropatterns (TRITC).
Image cells with DMSO only.
Focus on and image both the micropatterns and the labeled cell nuclei to identify single cells and ensure channel alignment.
Repeat at multiple positions in each of the 24 wells on the plate.
Take images with a 4x objective.
Export images as TIF files.
Open TIF files on a web-connected computer using ImageJ.
Ensure micropattern image names follow "sharedCoreName_pt.tif" format.
Ensure nuclei image names follow "sharedCoreName_dapi.tif" format.
Convert TIF images to PNG using ImageJ.
Load micropattern images into ImageJ as a stack.
Adjust brightness and contrast in Image > Adjust > Brightness/Contrast.
Smooth out the images.
Convert images to 8-bit using Image > Type > 8-bit.
Export images to PNG type with slice level as file name.
Create a new folder named "PNGs" and save PNG files there.
Repeat conversion process for nuclei images.
Upload PNG image pairs into image processing software for analysis.
Validate the account by contacting the authors.
Log into the software.
Under the Data tab on the left, click Upload Batch.
Import the images by dragging and dropping image pairs into the window that pops up and name the batch.
Click OK.
Check the box next to the batch name and click Analyze.
On the next screen, scroll down and check the box next to Contractility Analysis and click Select.
Lower down the page, select 10x as the magnification that was used for imaging from a drop-down menu.
Click Submit.
Once the data analysis reads Completed, click on the batch name.
On the next screen, click Download Data on the right side of the page.
Plot contraction values against drug concentrations to generate a concentration-response curve.
Determine the relative potencies of different treatments.
